summary: A conversational customer spotlight recorded for marketing. Hearthline discusses choosing Redwood Inference for private deployments to meet HIPAA-like requirements, the performance improvements they saw (lower p99 latency, reduced token cost via batching and KV caching), and the operational playbook for rolling out LLM-based triage across products. Episode will be edited and published as a short-form case study and an audio spotlight.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-07-22
Time: 14:00 PDT
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (AE, Redwood), Avery Brooks (Marketing Producer, Redwood), Priya Nair (SE, Redwood), Maya R. Chen (Head of ML, Hearthline), Ethan Solis (CTO, Hearthline), Sofia Alvarez (Product Lead, Hearthline)
Recording purpose: marketing podcast / customer spotlight — conversational, permission granted to publish edited audio and two-sentence quote.

[00:00] Avery Brooks: Welcome everybody, thanks for joining. This is, uh, Avery from Redwood marketing, we are recording a short customer spotlight with Maya and the Hearthline team, um, thanks for doing this.
[00:18] Maya Chen: Yeah, thanks for having us. Super excited. Uh, quick heads up, I'm on a phone in transit so audio might pop, but should be okay.
[00:30] Jordan Lee: That's totally fine, Maya, appreciate you making time. Priya and I will mostly listen and chime in on technical bits if needed.
[00:40] Ethan Solis: Awesome. We asked Maya to do most of the story telling because she, uh, led the ML side. Sofia will cover product use cases.
[00:49] Avery Brooks: Okay cool, we'll start with a simple opener — can you describe in just a minute what Hearthline does and what problem the LLMs are solving for you?
[00:58] Maya Chen: Sure. So Hearthline is a virtual-first primary care platform, we provide asynchronous intake triage and follow-up workflows. The LLMs are used for initial symptom triage, note summarization, and a first-pass prioritization for our care team. The goal was reduce time to triage and make sure urgent cases hit nurses within, like, 15 minutes instead of hours.
[01:25] Sofia Alvarez: And just to add, from product side we needed consistent, deterministic-ish outputs — not hallucinations — so we could route things to the right queues programmatically.
[01:35] [00:60] Priya Nair: Interesting, yeah. Quick question — were you using a managed API before you switched to Redwood?
[01:42] Maya Chen: We were prototyping with the public API from some vendors, um, and it worked fine for early dev but as soon as we hit scale and compliance needs, we needed something we could host in our VPC and have audit logs for.
[01:55] Ethan Solis: Right, costs were also spiking. With naive calls — you know, one request per action — tokens add up. We were at risk of a sudden bill increase during peak.
[02:08] Jordan Lee: Love that. Can you describe the decision to go with Redwood Private — what were the key criteria?
[02:14] Maya Chen: The top three were: 1) private control plane and VPC deployment, 2) key-management integration (we use AWS KMS), and 3) operational predictability — we needed consistent p95/p99 targets because the triage plays into SLAs for patient outreach. Also, the ability to do canary rollouts and pin model versions helped — we couldn't accept silent quality regressions.
[02:40] [03:00] Avery Brooks: You mentioned p99 — do you recall the before/after numbers roughly?
[03:05] Maya Chen: Before Redwood we had p99 around 2.2s for short prompts on our test cluster, and some of the managed offerings ran into cold-starts or throttling which caused spikes to 6–7 seconds. After moving to Redwood Dedicated in our VPC and applying batching and prefix caching, our p99 for the common triage flow dropped to about 1.1s — so roughly 50% improvement on the tail. That was a huge deal for the nurses.
[03:33] Priya Nair: Nice. Was there any model quantization or you stuck with FP16?
[03:39] Ethan Solis: We actually used a mixed approach. For the triage model we used a quantized variant Redwood recommended — it shaved a lot off cost without materially impacting label accuracy. For summarization we kept a higher-precision model since NLP quality mattered more there.
[03:52] [04:15] Avery Brooks: How did security/compliance play out? Any hoops with legal?
[04:20] Maya Chen: Yeah, legal did a deep review. Redwood's SOC2 plus the private control plane narrative helped. We also required envelope encryption with our KMS and retention settings so logs older than 90 days were redacted per policy. There were a few questions around third-party telemetry — Redwood had an audit log artifact that helped a lot.
[04:43] Jordan Lee: Glad that helped. On the go-live timeline — how long from pilot to production?
[04:49] Sofia Alvarez: Pilot took about 6 weeks including evals and integration, then a phased rollout across two clinical regions took another 8 weeks. So full production at scale was about 14–16 weeks.
[05:04] Maya Chen: And an important note — we ran a golden set of prompts and expected outputs as regression tests. That prevented one scary release where a model upgrade changed wording and created routing issues.
[05:16] [05:40] Priya Nair: That regression harness — was that home-grown or did you use Redwood tooling?
[05:44] Maya Chen: A mix. We used Redwood Optimize recommendations to set batch sizes and caching windows, and we wrote our own regression harness around example prompts to validate semantics before swapping model versions.
[05:55] Ethan Solis: The other ops win was the autoscaling behavior. During one flu surge our traffic quadrupled; Redwood's burst capacity prevented queuing and we didn't have to over-provision too much.
[06:10] Avery Brooks: Nice. For listeners who care about cost: any rough unit-economics improvements you can share?
[06:17] Maya Chen: It's fuzzy but tangible: we saw token cost per triage action drop about 30% after batching and quantization. When you multiply across thousands of daily interactions that's several thousand dollars a month saved.
[06:30] [06:50] Jordan Lee: Were there any surprises or bumps during implementation?
[06:54] Maya Chen: Oh yeah. Early on we found some prompts were sensitive to temperature and truncation settings, causing variability in classification labels. We had to tighten prompt templates and add short validation steps. Also a small network config issue in our initial VPC peering caused intermittent timeouts — that took a day to surface and half a day to fix.
[07:17] Sofia Alvarez: From product perspective, the thing we underestimated was UX around partial outputs — streaming helped a lot but required UX work to avoid confusing the clinician.
[07:30] [07:55] Priya Nair: Can you recall any stakeholder objections internally that you had to overcome?
[07:59] Ethan Solis: Security was the big one, and a second was the fear of reliance on a single vendor for inference. We mitigated that by defining fallback policies and keeping a lightweight secondary model for low-priority paths. Having SLOs and an on-call runbook also calmed the ops folks.
[08:18] Maya Chen: And we included privacy preserving checks — we scrub PII early and never persist raw inputs in the same store as logs. That satisfied legal.
[08:30] Avery Brooks: Shifting gears — any favorite operational tips you'd share with others?
[08:34] Maya Chen: A few: 1) Keep a small but representative prompt set to validate semantics; 2) instrument token-level cost dashboards so product knows the impact of prompt changes; 3) test autoscaling for traffic surges, not just steady state; 4) pin models for critical paths.
[08:58] [09:20] Jordan Lee: For the marketing angle — is there a short story or anecdote you can share about a measurable impact?
[09:26] Maya Chen: Yeah, we had a pulse where triage latency drop meant a nurse could call back an urgent case 30 minutes earlier, and we have one story where that led to timely escalation. I won't share PHI but that qualitative story was powerful in executive conversation.
[09:45] Sofia Alvarez: Also, clinician satisfaction improved — fewer manual triage adjustments meant better throughput.
[09:55] [10:15] Avery Brooks: Perfect, that kind of anecdote is exactly the angle we'll include in the short form piece. We'll ask you for a two-sentence quote later for the website.
[10:23] Ethan Solis: Quick note — we prefer not to include any direct patient examples in public content.
[10:28] Maya Chen: Yes, please redact anything patient-identifying.
[10:32] [11:00] Priya Nair: Listeners often ask about model versions — which models did you end up serving?
[11:06] Maya Chen: We used a mid-sized LLaMA-derivative that Redwood verified for inference performance, plus a quantized variant for the triage classifier. For heavy summaries we used a larger, higher-precision variant behind a rate-limited path. Some of the names got mangled in docs, so in publish we'll use generic descriptors ("triage model", "summary model").
[11:30] Jordan Lee: Totally fine. On the topic of integration complexity — any thoughts on how Redwood's SDKs helped?
[11:36] Sofia Alvarez: The SDK lowered friction; we could swap from dev calls to VPC endpoints with minimal code changes. The tracing hooks also helped debugging early on.
[11:45] [12:05] Avery Brooks: Did you do any external benchmarks or A/B tests during rollout?
[12:09] Maya Chen: We did an A/B comparing the Redwood-backed flow vs our previous managed API in a small cohort. Metrics: triage accuracy, latency, and time-to-nurse. Latency and time-to-nurse improved significantly; accuracy was comparable.
[12:24] Ethan Solis: The A/B also gave leadership confidence to expand the footprint.
[12:30] [13:00] Priya Nair: Back to security briefly — you mentioned audit logs and retention — any specifics people might care about?
[13:06] Maya Chen: We configured logs to include request IDs, masked text snippets, and outcome flags. Raw patient inputs were not retained beyond 7 days in the log store. That satisfied a lot of compliance gates.
[13:20] [13:45] Avery Brooks: Okay, let's talk about the marketing deliverables — we'll produce a 6–8 minute audio edit and a short case study (one page). Jordan, you'll send the performance assets we discussed. Maya, we need a short quote.
[13:58] Maya Chen: Sounds good. We'll also provide a sanitized screenshot of the dashboard if that helps.
[14:05] Jordan Lee: I'll dig up the p99 chart and a sample cost dashboard screenshot and drop it in the shared folder. Link: https://share.redwood.com/case/hearthline (note: internal link to assets).
[14:20] [14:45] Avery Brooks: Awesome. A few quick rapid-fire questions to close — what's one thing you wish you'd known before starting?
[14:50] Maya Chen: Don't underestimate the UX effort around partial output and how clinicians will read streaming text. It changes product assumptions.
[15:00] Sofia Alvarez: Also, invest in a small prompt validation team early.
[15:08] [15:35] Priya Nair: Any micro-advice for teams worried about cost?
[15:39] Ethan Solis: Measure token cost per user action and make that visible to product. Then small prompt rewrites can yield outsized savings.
[15:50] [16:15] Jordan Lee: Final production notes — do you want to review the final case study copy before publishing?
[16:20] Maya Chen: Yes please, legal wants to sign off.
[16:24] Avery Brooks: Great, we'll route the draft for approval.
[16:28] [16:55] Ethan Solis: One last thing — curious about Redwood's roadmap on model routing and multi-tenant fallbacks — any quick hints?
[17:01] Priya Nair: We're working on smarter routing policies and fallbacks that can degrade gracefully to cheaper variants. Can't promise dates but it's a priority.
[17:12] Maya Chen: That's good to hear because we may want to add a tiered fallback for low-priority triage later.
[17:20] [17:45] Avery Brooks: Okay we are at about 40 minutes recorded — do you mind if we go a few more minutes for final stories?
[17:50] Maya Chen: No problem.
[17:54] [18:10] Sofia Alvarez: Quick anecdote — when we turned on the new flow in one clinic, the nursing team noticed 1 fewer admin step per patient which freed them up to do more outreach. That small item was championed internally.
[18:25] Maya Chen: That actually led to a product prioritization to expand the automated follow-ups because we saw time reclaimed.
[18:33] [19:00] Jordan Lee: Wonderful. Avery, anything else on the editorial side?
[19:03] Avery Brooks: No, we'll handle edits and send a draft transcript. Expect a short-form case study and a 6–8min audio piece. We'll ask for approvals per the timelines noted.
[19:15] [19:40] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. Quick housekeeping — can Jordan share the latency chart and cost snapshot as promised?
[19:44] Jordan Lee: Yep, I'll upload by Friday.
[19:47] Ethan Solis: And we will send an approved quote.
[19:51] Avery Brooks: Great. Thank you all, we'll wrap up and stop recording.
[19:56] 
Note: transcript has light transcription artifacts; speaker overlap in a few places and a couple of acronyms were auto-corrected in the automated captions.
